documents.title: AMSSM Position Statement on Concussion in Sport

chunks.content: INTRODUCTION Approximately 60 to 70 million cases of traumatic brain injury (TBI) occur worldwide annually, with 73% to 90% classified as mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Due to its high prevalence and frequently underestimated sequelae, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention considers concussion a major public health concern. Vestibular symptoms are common following TBI. Peripheral vestibular structures can be damaged at the level of the labyrinth or the vestibular nerve. Post-concussive vestibular dysfunction (PCVD) results from damage to peripheral structures (labyrinth or vestibular nerve) and central pathways within the brainstem, cerebellum, and supratentorial vestibular cortex. Although macrostructural damage is rarer in mTBI than in moderate and severe TBI, microstructural white matter abnormalities and diffuse axonal injury are frequently reported. In pediatric and sports medicine, the prevalence of vestibular dysfunction reaches up to 81%, with dizziness reported by 67%–77% of patients during the acute phase. It is well documented that initial presentation of dizziness is one predictor of a protracted recovery following concussion. The functional scope of the vestibular system extends beyond mere visual and balance control to encompass various domains such as self-orientation, sensory organization, and sensory weighting. The complexity of PCVD may also be associated with cervical or temporomandibular joint dysfunction. This review investigates the mechanisms, assessment, and differential diagnosis of PCVD, alongside evidence-based rehabilitation protocols and the latest advancements in technology, aiming to provide clinical insights to maximize patient recovery. MECHANISMS AND PATHOPHYSIOLOGY illustrates a brief schematic of the integrated pathophysiology. Peripheral vestibular injury Peripheral vestibular disorders range from common conditions such as benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) to less common causes including labyrinthine concussion, perilymphatic fistulas, endolymphatic hydrops, and temporal bone fractures. Other less common conditions are post-traumatic Meniere’s syndrome and direct damage to the vestibular nerve itself. Inferior vestibular nerve damage, often resulting from traumatic nerve stretching, is a frequently overlooked mechanism of PCVD. While difficult to detect via conventional exams, it can be elucidated through vestibular evoked myogenic potentials and high-precision imaging; thus, clinical suspicion should warrant otolaryngologic referral for accurate diagnosis. Furthermore, otolith organs may be more vulnerable to mTBI than semicircular canals, leading to severe dizziness even with normal vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) tests. In such cases, specialized rehabilitation focusing on postural control and spatial orientation must be integrated with conventional VOR-based exercises to optimize recovery. Central vestibular injury Anatomically, the vestibular system connects inner ear organs with the brainstem, cerebellum, and the parieto-insular vestibular cortex (PIVC), linking closely with the ocular system and postural muscles. Concussions cause extensive microstructural disruption of white matter channels including the cerebellar peduncles rather than localized lesions. Previous imaging has demonstrated volume reduction in the brainstem and decreased fractional anisotropy in the corpus callosum, leading to pervasive damage in networks regulating vestibulo-ocular and vestibulo-spinal reflexes (VSRs). Higher-order vestibular functions are mediated by complex networks integrating multisensory information with feedback and feedforward cognitive control. Vestibular signals project beyond the frontal and parietal lobes to the medial temporal lobe and hippocampus, forming a comprehensive cerebral connectivity that is often disrupted in PCVD. As the cerebellum, especially vestibulocerebellum, is a critical structure that regulates motor responses by integrating vestibular, visual, and proprioceptive inputs, dysfunction in this region leads to persistent imbalance, dizziness, and gaze instability. Furthermore, the frontal lobe, which is highly vulnerable to concussive forces, governs higher-order oculomotor control. Deficits in the spatial mapping process—a critical precursor to conscious attention—lead to reduced accuracy and efficiency in both saccades and smooth pursuits. Dysfunctional sensory integration and pathological visual dependency Normal balance relies on the dynamic modulation of multisensory inputs. However, patients with chronic mTBI often struggle with central sensory integration. Unlike those in the acute phase, chronic PCVD patients fail to preferentially process vestibular and somatosensory signals when visual information is unavailable. This suggests that visual dependency in chronic mTBI is a long-term deficit in multisensory processing rather than a simple compensatory strategy, likely due to disrupted connectivity within the PIVC and multisensory hubs. Furthermore, post-concussion hyperactivation of the visual cortex and abnormal vestibulo-limbic interactions via the parabrachial nucleus can exacerbate the psychological fixation of dizziness, potentially transitioning acute instability into persistent post-concussive symptoms (PPCS) or chronic phobic postural vertigo. These mechanisms underscore why active sensory reorganization—rather than simple symptom-suppressing medication—is essential for mTBI recovery. While vestibular suppressants provide temporary relief, they may hinder neuroplasticity. Conversely, habituation and sensory re-weighting training facilitate the resolution of pathological visual dependency and restructure damaged PIVC connectivity. By promoting neural adaptation through repetitive exposure, these strategies optimize multisensory integration and prevent progression into chronic psychogenic vertigo. Additionally, central vestibular injury may cause vestibular agnosia, where the brain fails to recognize body movement. This can lead to frequent falls and clinical oversight, as patients may be unaware of their dysfunction. Therefore, evaluating PCVD requires a comprehensive approach that correlates objective test results with subjective reports.

By promoting neural adaptation through repetitive exposure, these strategies optimize multisensory integration and prevent progression into chronic psychogenic vertigo. Additionally, central vestibular injury may cause vestibular agnosia, where the brain fails to recognize body movement. This can lead to frequent falls and clinical oversight, as patients may be unaware of their dysfunction. Therefore, evaluating PCVD requires a comprehensive approach that correlates objective test results with subjective reports. Cervicogenic contributions to PCVD Concussive acceleration-deceleration forces often cause cervical spine injuries, such as whiplash. The upper cervical spine possesses a high density of muscle spindles, and traumatic changes—including inflammation and fatty infiltration—alter their sensitivity. This distortion of proprioceptive afferent information results in sensory mismatch, which is further exacerbated by chronic neck pain and sympathetic activation. Consequently, a vicious cycle of persistent pain and postural instability develops. These ‘false signals’ originating from the neck, the body’s balance control system misses the proper timing, causing confusion in the information integration process. This interference with the tuning of the VOR and VSR can lead to secondary gaze instability, and visual disturbance, causing patients to experience an unstable visual field and difficulty with fixation. Psychological dimensions and persistent positional-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) PPPD is a chronic vestibular dysfunction characterized by impaired central processing of balance information following concussion or whiplash, accounting for 10%–15% of all PPPD cases. Beyond non-rotational vertigo—often described as cloudiness or heaviness—patients suffer from persistent instability and hypersensitivity to visual and somatosensory stimuli. The core mechanism involves the brain misinterpreting ordinary environmental stimuli as 'danger,' leading to a sustained, maladaptive vertigo response. Clinicians frequently overlook the critical interplay between vestibular anxiety and kinesiophobia in PPPD patients during routine evaluations. These psychological factors are not merely secondary; they actively exacerbate vestibular symptoms via neural circuits that bridge the amygdala, the limbic system, and the vestibular nuclei. Notably, those struggling with kinesiophobia often resort to protective avoidance behaviors, such as rigid head fixation. Such immobilization effectively mutes the 'sensory-error signals' that the brain relies on for self-calibration. By depriving the nervous system of these essential inputs, this restriction directly stalls habituation and adaptation—the very pillars of vestibular compensation—thereby anchoring the patient in a state of delayed recovery. In the post-concussion context, PPPD may arise de novo from disrupted sensory reweighting or be directly precipitated by the acute vestibular event itself. Alternatively, the condition may be precipitated by the acute vestibular insult itself. Therefore, clinicians should maintain a high index of suspicion for PPPD in patients presenting with chronic, treatment-resistant dizziness, particularly when symptoms are exacerbated by visually demanding environments or sustained upright posture. NATURAL HISTORY AND PROGNOSIS PCVD typically improves during the acute phase; however, approximately one-third of untreated athletes with mTBI develop chronic symptoms. Moreover, as physiological vestibular dysfunction may persist even after subjective symptoms subside, careful follow-up is essential. The cognitive and emotional symptoms and reduced occupational performance associated with PPCS-often exacerbated by persistent PCVD-compromise social roles, causing patients to experience a ‘loss of self’ and significant changes in identity. Notably, the TRACK-TBI study confirmed that 26% of patients reported persistent symptoms even one year post-injury, suggesting that long-term PCVD is by no means a rare sequela and warrants targeted intervention. Early clinical evidence of vestibular-oculomotor dysfunction is associated with a 4-fold increased risk of developing persistent symptoms. Factors such as impaired VOR, a history of concussion, underlying psychiatric disorders, and onset in female patients are closely associated with delayed recovery. These findings emphasize that PCVD is a marker of substantial functional impairment rather than a mere subjective complaint. Therefore, determining a safe return to daily activities or sports should be based on objective evaluations of vestibular function than relying solely on the patient's self-reports. Cervicogenic contributions are also important prognostic markers, because cervical symptoms affect up to 90% of chronic mTBI patients. Initial neck pain increases the risk of prolonged recovery, often due to sensory mismatch where distorted proprioceptive signals from the injured upper cervical spine conflict with visual and vestibular inputs. This disharmony often involves cervical strain and impaired central sensory integration, can lead to maladaptive sensory reweighting if not addressed early. VESTIBULAR ASSESSMENT AND DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS Vestibular assessment A comprehensive evaluation begins with a bedside neurologic examination that evaluates vergence, fixation stability, and alignment. The pattern of nystagmus is a key indicator for differential diagnosis: horizontal and direction-fixed nystagmus suggest unilateral peripheral vestibular dysfunction. Conversely, vertical or rotational nystagmus, or gaze-evoked nystagmus indicates a central lesion. Utilizing Frenzel lenses or video nystagmography enhance diagnostic reliability. VESTIBULAR ASSESSMENT AND DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS Vestibular assessment A comprehensive evaluation begins with a bedside neurologic examination that evaluates vergence, fixation stability, and alignment. The pattern of nystagmus is a key indicator for differential diagnosis: horizontal and direction-fixed nystagmus suggest unilateral peripheral vestibular dysfunction. Conversely, vertical or rotational nystagmus, or gaze-evoked nystagmus indicates a central lesion. Utilizing Frenzel lenses or video nystagmography enhance diagnostic reliability. For sport-related concussions, the Vestibular Ocular Motor Screening efficiently evaluate smooth pursuit, saccades, near point of convergence, VOR, and visual motion sensitivity, serving as a valuable predictor of recovery duration. Additionally, the King-Devick Test provides a rapid screening for saccadic eye movements and suboptimal brain function through timed rapid number naming. Assessment of static and dynamic balance is essential to determine functional status. Standard measures include the Sensory Organization Test, which measures integration abilities, its simplified version, modified Clinical Test of Sensory Interaction on Balance, and the Balance Error Scoring System (BESS). However, the BESS may have low discriminative power for high-level athletes due to the ceiling effect. Dynamic balance and gait function can be evaluated using the tandem gait task and motion analysis. Patient-reported outcomes are captured using the Dizziness Handicap Inventory (DHI), which quantifies functional, emotional, and physical impacts of symptoms. Advanced diagnostic tests or imaging such as video head impulse test, vestibular evoked myogenic potential, and magnetic resonance imaging, are not routinely indicated, they should be considered for worsening symptoms, inconclusive bedside findings, or suspected structural lesions. Differential diagnosis Differential diagnosis of vestibular dysfunction and dizziness following mTBI are summarized in . It is important to note that whiplash injury, concussion, and cervicogenic dizziness are not mutually exclusive diagnoses and often coexist. As no “gold standard” exists for cervicogenic dizziness, diagnosis relies on both the exclusion of other neuro-otological disorders and the presence of clinical findings such as neck pain, restricted range of motion (ROM), cervical tenderness, and dizziness induced by passive neck rotation. Consequently, a basic cervical examination—assessing pain, ROM, and radiculopathy—should precede the full vestibular workup. If cervical movement is limited, subsequent vestibular tests must be modified accordingly. The head-neck differentiation test (seated cervical rotation test) is a useful tool for distinguishing cervicogenic from vestibular components. If dizziness is elicited by rotating the torso while the head remains fixed (using a swivel chair), a cervical origin is suspected; conversely, dizziness during simultaneous head and torso rotation suggests a vestibular etiology. In the chronic phase, differentiation is crucial because patients with vestibular migraine or PPPD are highly sensitive to visual stimuli. PRINCIPLES OF VESTIBULAR REHABILITATION: ADAPTATION, SUBSTITUTION, AND HABITUATION Symptoms of vestibular dysfunction, such as nystagmus and postural asymmetry, often resolve through central vestibular compensation. This process involves the central nervous system's plasticity to re-establish equilibrium between bilateral vestibular nuclei. While spontaneous recovery is common, targeted VRT is indicated for persistent PCVD. Notably, acute-phase medications can suppress the central nervous system, hindering neuroplasticity; thus, minimizing drug use and encouraging early activity are crucial. VRT is fundamentally based on three pillars: adaptation, substitution, and habituation ( ). In bilateral vestibular loss, the cervico-ocular reflex provides limited compensation (typically ≤0.5 Hz). Therefore, for high-frequency stability (e.g., walking), combining adaptive training to maximize residual function is more effective than relying solely on substitution. Beyond these fundamental pillars, specific strategies are required for cerebellar lesions and vestibular disinhibition. Since the cerebellum acts as an 'inhibitory brake' on vestibular output, its impairment often results in VOR disinhibition. In such cases, VOR suppression training is essential to restore cerebellar regulation. Additionally, VOR memory training (remembered target training) can be implemented to enhance internal predictive models and spatial memory by having patients visualize targets during head movements with their eyes closed. VESTIBULAR REHABILITATION PRACTICE A patient-specific approach VRT must be tailored to specific functional deficits and symptom-provoking factors. The key is to adjust intensity according to symptom response and functional tolerance rather than adhering to a fixed schedule. While mild symptom induction is permissible, the treatment focuses on systematic adaptation through graded exposure within an acceptable range. Furthermore, VRT should be directly linked to functional goals (e.g., community ambulation, driving, or returning to sports) and monitored accordingly. Finally, optimal outcomes are achieved when VRT is implemented within a comprehensive multidisciplinary framework that includes patient education and pacing strategies. Recent guidelines (e.g., 2021 JAMA Network Open) suggest systematic information provision, progressive aerobic exercise, vestibular rehabilitation, and manual therapy for the non-pharmacological treatment of PPCS; however, the level of recommendation was weak due to low certainty of evidence. Clinicians should prioritize shared decision-making tailored to the individual rather than relying on a rigid protocol. Importantly, a lack of objective improvement should prompt a multidisciplinary review of the diagnosis to prevent entrenching maladaptive illness behaviors, rather than simply extending

Recent guidelines (e.g., 2021 JAMA Network Open) suggest systematic information provision, progressive aerobic exercise, vestibular rehabilitation, and manual therapy for the non-pharmacological treatment of PPCS; however, the level of recommendation was weak due to low certainty of evidence. Clinicians should prioritize shared decision-making tailored to the individual rather than relying on a rigid protocol. Importantly, a lack of objective improvement should prompt a multidisciplinary review of the diagnosis to prevent entrenching maladaptive illness behaviors, rather than simply extending existing exercises. Timing of referral and initiation The paradigm is shifting from traditional ‘symptom stabilization’ toward early intervention as soon as dysfunction is identified. Early referrals to vestibulo-ocular and cervicovestibular therapy can accelerate symptom resolution and return to sports. In adolescents, starting individualized rehabilitation within 21 days of onset has shown significantly superior recovery compared to simple observation. If no signs of natural recovery are observed during the subacute period, immediate referral is necessary to prevent chronicity. Clinicians must avoid ‘clinical inertia’—neglecting the condition when recovery deviates from the expected path. Therapeutic dosing in vestibular rehabilitation According to the updated clinical practice guidelines from the Academy of Neurologic Physical Therapy of the American Physical Therapy Association, patients with chronic unilateral vestibular hypofunction should perform balance exercises for at least 20 minutes daily for 4–6 weeks, and 6–9 weeks for bilateral cases. While the necessity of exercise is acknowledged for acute and subacute patients, specific dosage recommendations remain undefined. For gaze stabilization exercises, it is recommended that acute/subacute unilateral patients exercise for at least 12 minutes per day (divided into three sessions), while chronic unilateral patients should aim for at least 20 minutes per day (divided into 3 to 5 sessions) for 4 to 6 weeks. Notably, patients with bilateral vestibular hypofunction are advised to exercise for 20 to 40 minutes per day over 5 to 7 weeks. Previous research has noted that repeating brief unidirectional optokinetic stimulation for 30 seconds, approximately 10 times daily, can induce changes in VOR gain. This suggests that even short periods of stimulation, when performed repeatedly, can sufficiently promote the recovery of vestibular function. To enhance adherence, clinicians should integrate exercises into daily activities to mitigate boredom and discomfort. Cervicovestibular rehabilitation Manual therapy, particularly focused on the upper cervical spine, significantly improves dizziness intensity and its impact on daily life compared to control or placebo treatments. However, the level of evidence for other clinical indicators remains insufficient; the certainty of evidence for pain intensity, cervical ROM, and disability indices was assessed as ‘low’ or ‘very low.’ This suggests that while manual therapy effectively alleviates specific symptoms, further robust evidence is needed to confirm its overall clinical impact. Multimodal interventions—combining cervical manual therapy with vestibular and/or oculomotor exercises—are superior to monotherapy for achieving faster clinical improvement and return to sport, particularly in persistent cases. For instance, treating cervical dysfunction and BPPV within three weeks of injury, followed by visual-vestibular integration therapy, significantly improves both objective and subjective outcomes in patients with comorbid cervicogenic headache and vestibular deficits. However, cervicovestibular rehabilitation is not a panacea. A randomized clinical trial showed that adding this therapy to symptom-limited aerobic exercise provided no superior benefit in subjective symptoms (e.g., pain, dizziness, headache) or functional recovery speed compared to aerobic exercise alone. Conversely, the combined group showed a clear advantage in objective measures, such as VOR and craniovertebral mobility. Thus, concurrent cervicovestibular rehabilitation and VRT are specifically indicated for patients with confirmed VOR impairment or limited cervical mobility. Psychological and anxiety dimensions in PPPD Standard VRT protocols are often less effective for PPPD than for structural lesions, as many patients discontinue conventional habituation due to symptom exacerbation. This underscores the necessity of an anxiety-informed, modified rehabilitation approach. Baseline anxiety and depression are independent negative predictors of VRT outcomes; a higher psychological burden significantly attenuates functional recovery, as measured by the DHI. Evidence-based treatment for vestibular anxiety and PPPD requires a multifaceted approach. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is designed to correct maladaptive beliefs and movement avoidance behaviors associated with dizziness. With follow-up results of up to six months, CBT significantly reduced DHI scores and anxiety levels. Therefore, if factors that may psychologically exacerbate PPPD patients are identified, CBT must be included as a core treatment element of VRT. Graded exposure—the systematic, desensitized reintroduction of symptom-provoking activities in a controlled, progressively challenging sequence—serves as the behavioral backbone of this approach. Meta-analytic evidence further supports that the combination of SSRIs or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors with structured VRT yields superior outcomes in DHI score reduction and anxiety compared to either modality in isolation; however, current evidence from placebo-controlled randomized trials remains limited, necessitating individualized risk-benefit assessment for pharmacological adjuncts. Graded exposure—the systematic, desensitized reintroduction of symptom-provoking activities in a controlled, progressively challenging sequence—serves as the behavioral backbone of this approach. Meta-analytic evidence further supports that the combination of SSRIs or serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors with structured VRT yields superior outcomes in DHI score reduction and anxiety compared to either modality in isolation; however, current evidence from placebo-controlled randomized trials remains limited, necessitating individualized risk-benefit assessment for pharmacological adjuncts. When VRT progress plateaus or patients demonstrate marked avoidance behavior, clinicians should formally assess for comorbid PPPD or vestibular anxiety using validated instruments such as the Niigata PPPD Questionnaire or the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Scale. These conditions should be managed through coordinated neuropsychiatric consultation, rather than simply escalating the exercise dose or extending treatment duration. EMERGING TECHNOLOGIES AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS Virtual reality (VR) VR platforms represent one of the most rapidly evolving fields in vestibular rehabilitation, effectively suppressing ‘visual vertigo’ by inducing habituation through exposure to complex visual environments. Although studies on concussion patients indicate that VR-based rehabilitation improves balance, gait, and functional outcomes, the overall quality of evidence is currently categorized as low. A recent meta-analysis indicates that VR-assisted therapy significantly improves DHI scores compared to conventional therapy, particularly in peripheral disorders; however, high heterogeneity and limited efficacy in central disorders necessitate further large-scale validation. To address these limitations, recent research has focused on enhancing ecological validity and objective monitoring. For instance, the Praxis system utilizes a military-specific VR framework combined with wearable sensors to detect subtle vestibular deficits that traditional assessments often miss. This technology-driven approach aims to optimize recovery tracking and refine return-to-duty criteria for service members with mTBI. Similarly, a case study of a collegiate football player demonstrated that a 10-week intervention using VR and force-plate technology significantly improved both objective stability and subjective post-concussion symptoms. These advancements illustrate the potential of immersive, data-driven platforms to provide standardized, high-sensitivity rehabilitation that bridges the gap between clinical settings and real-world functional demands. These advancements are further supported by the increasing accessibility of high-performance, cost-effective VR hardware, which has transitioned from specialized research tools to broader clinical application. Nevertheless, the current literature has yet to establish optimal patient selection, standardized treatment durations, or the definitive additive benefit of VR over well-designed conventional therapy. Wearables and biofeedback Wearable technology enables precise movement quantification and real-time feedback beyond clinical settings. For instance, the Vertigenius™ system utilizes a retroauricular sensor and mobile app to monitor eye stabilization exercises and manage dizziness indicators remotely. Similarly, audio biofeedback (ABF) systems provide auditory cues for postural correction; in chronic mTBI, an randomized controlled trial demonstrated that VR with ABF significantly enhances motor activation and reduces response time delays compared to standard therapy. Wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) further provide an objective means to monitor home-based exercise quality. In 73 patients with mTBI, IMU-derived metrics revealed slower peak forehead angular velocity and increased ROM compared to controls, suggesting compensatory strategies and impaired proprioception, respectively. Building on this, the ongoing SuBTyPE trial utilizes a multidimensional biofeedback system to establish normative mobility profiles in military personnel, laying the groundwork for future precision rehabilitation. Beyond simple monitoring, the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) with continuous wearable sensor data opens new possibilities for precision vestibular rehabilitation. ML models applied to large-scale postural datasets can stratify patients into distinct recovery phenotypes; for instance, analysis of center-of-pressure entropy metrics in post-concussion vestibular dysfunction has identified statistically significant reductions in signal complexity under sensory-conflict conditions, providing data-driven biomarkers to guide individualized intervention strategies. AI-driven digital therapeutics can further translate these insights into closed-loop exercise systems that dynamically modulate task parameters—such as target velocity or amplitude in gaze stabilization tasks—based on real-time performance feedback, rather than fixed dose-escalation protocols. These dynamic systems facilitate individualized, home-based rehabilitation by adjusting to the patient's recovery progress in real-time, reducing dependence on on-site supervision while maintaining therapeutic efficacy, though challenges including long-term patient engagement and digital health literacy warrant continued attention. Smartphone-based tools Recent advancements allow for the remote, quantitative assessment of postural instability in concussion patients using smartphone accelerometers. Studies demonstrate that balance data collected under various surface and visual conditions significantly distinguish concussion patients from healthy controls. Such objective metrics provide practical utility in monitoring recovery trajectories and informing return-to-sport decisions. Emerging adjunctive technologies Complementary therapies using vibrotactile feedback and electrical vestibular stimulation are gaining traction in vestibular rehabilitation. Vibrotactile feedback, often integrated with gamification, addresses the poor compliance associated with repetitive conventional VOR exercises. Wearable devices, such as “StableEyes” provide real-time vibration cues when head movement speed or angle deviates from targets. By integrating simultaneous visual and tactile inputs, these systems enhance multisensory compensation for

Such objective metrics provide practical utility in monitoring recovery trajectories and informing return-to-sport decisions. Emerging adjunctive technologies Complementary therapies using vibrotactile feedback and electrical vestibular stimulation are gaining traction in vestibular rehabilitation. Vibrotactile feedback, often integrated with gamification, addresses the poor compliance associated with repetitive conventional VOR exercises. Wearable devices, such as “StableEyes” provide real-time vibration cues when head movement speed or angle deviates from targets. By integrating simultaneous visual and tactile inputs, these systems enhance multisensory compensation for impaired vestibular function, leading to improved VOR gain even after brief training periods. Limitations and future directions Current research on vestibular rehabilitation technologies faces limitations in establishing robust levels of evidence due to small sample sizes and high study heterogeneity. Consequently, future research must prioritize developing standardized, objective outcome measures and optimal treatment programs tailored to individual patient characteristics and recovery stages. Beyond research limitations, the practical implementation of VRT faces significant systemic barriers in certain healthcare environments, such as South Korea. Domestically, dedicated rehabilitation programs run by specialized physical therapists remain scarce due to structural constraints, including short outpatient consultation times, a lack of standardized therapist training, and insufficient insurance reimbursement for prolonged exercise-based therapies. To overcome both these scientific and structural limitations, future directions should strongly focus on an integrated, hybrid care model. By combining brief, physician-led education in the clinic with the active prescription of digital therapeutics—such as app-based VRT, wearable biofeedback, and remote monitoring—clinicians can effectively bypass temporal and spatial constraints. This technology-assisted, home-based approach provides a realistic pathway to deliver continuous, high-quality, and precise individualized treatment, ultimately maximizing vestibular recovery for patients with persistent post-concussion dizziness within resource-limited clinical environments. CONCLUSION Recently, clinical and research efforts for PCVD have shifted beyond symptomatic management toward “pathophysiology-centered precision rehabilitation.” This approach emphasizes evaluating the complex interactions between peripheral, central, and cervical systems to explain individual symptoms and provide tailored interventions. For effective recovery, individualized VRT programs should be initiated from the early stages, with specialized cervicovestibular programs integrated following a systematic differential diagnosis. Furthermore, the integration of cutting-edge technologies, such as VR and wearable sensors, into multidisciplinary assessment systems allows for more precise, data-driven treatment planning. By transitioning to these personalized and technology-enhanced strategies, clinicians can minimize the risk of long-term sequelae and optimize a successful, functional return to daily life and sports for patients with PCVD.

documents.title: AMSSM Position Statement on Cardiac Preparticipation Screening

chunks.content: Nonstandard Abbreviations and Acronyms ARENA Australasian Registry of Screening ECGs in National Athletes ARVC arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy SCD sudden cardiac death TWI T‐wave inversion TWI V2–3 T‐wave inversion in leads V 2 and V 3 Clinical Perspective What Is New? This study found that isolated T‐wave inversion in leads V 2 and V 3 was 4 times as common in female athletes compared with male athletes and nearly 5 times as common in endurance compared with nonendurance athletes. The finding of isolated T‐wave inversion in leads V 2 and V 3 was the most common ECG abnormality in female athletes and was not associated with cardiac pathology or major cardiac events in this large ECG data set in elite athletes. What Are the Clinical Implications? Our data support that isolated TWI V2–3 may be considered a normal ECG finding in asymptomatic female athletes, which would lower the false‐positive rate of ECG screening in female athletes. Cardiac screening of athletes is common internationally, although the exact protocol may vary. , , In Australia and New Zealand, organized programs for cardiac screening of young athletes occur only at the elite level. The Australasian College of Sport and Exercise Physicians position statement recommends preparticipation screening of athletes with a history, physical examination, and 12‐lead ECG on entry to an elite program and then every 2 years until the age of 25 years. “Elite athletes” are those playing in professional competitions, in national or state institutes of sport, and others for whom sports training and competition is their primary activity. Most individual sporting organizations in Australia and New Zealand have a cardiac screening policy; these are largely uniform, commencing at age 15 to 17 years. Female athletes are reported to have a higher proportion of abnormal screening ECGs, , , despite a rate of sudden cardiac death (SCD) that is 4 to 10 times lower than in male athletes. , , , Female athletes have a higher prevalence of T‐wave inversion in leads V 2 and V 3 (TWI V2–3 ) than male athletes, which is often not associated with cardiac pathology. , , , Endurance athletes also are reported to have a higher prevalence of TWI V2–3 than nonendurance athletes. , , TWI V2–3 is considered abnormal for athletes aged ≥16 years in the International Criteria for Athlete ECG Interpretation due to its association with cardiomyopathies, including arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. TWI in leads V 1 , V 2 , and V 3 in individuals aged ≥14 years (in the absence of complete right bundle‐branch block [RBBB]) is a major criterion for diagnosis of the right ventricular phenotype of arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ARVC) according to the Marcus criteria and the 2024 European Task Force criteria. This study aimed to determine (1) the prevalence of isolated TWI V2–3 in different sexes and sporting disciplines and (2) whether isolated TWI V2–3 is associated with clinical pathology using a large data set of elite athlete screening ECGs from Australia and New Zealand. Methods Cardiac screening records of elite athletes were obtained from the ARENA (Australasian Registry of ECGs of National Athletes) project and combined with previous athlete cohort studies conducted by the research team in Australia , and New Zealand. Methods for these studies have been previously reported. , , Briefly, retrospective and prospective data were collected from each participating sporting organization and included demographic information, screening ECGs and results, details of any follow‐up testing, diagnoses, and major adverse cardiac outcomes. , , , Retrospective data covered all available records since the commencement of the sporting organization's cardiac screening policy (generally from 2012 to 2015) until the date of collection (2022–2024). Athletes were included if a copy of the ECG from the study period was available and they were aged <40 years at the time of screening. Athletes were screened with personal and family history, physical examination, and resting 12‐lead ECG. Follow‐up testing and evaluation was conducted if required by each sporting organization. ECGs were interpreted at the time they were undertaken by sports physicians, general practitioners, or cardiologists with expertise in athlete ECG interpretation using contemporary athlete‐specific ECG criteria. All ECGs were re‐reviewed by a member of the research team in accordance with the International Criteria for Athlete ECG Interpretation. All abnormal ECGs and all ECGs with contradictory interpretation between the original screening physician and the research team underwent additional review by 2 expert sports cardiologists, and in the event of a disagreement, the majority view was used. Athletes were considered to have an abnormal ECG if they had at least 1 ECG requiring further evaluation (abnormal or with ≥2 borderline findings) according to the International Criteria. If athletes had >1 abnormal ECG, only the first was included in the analyses. Athletes were considered isolated TWI V2–3 cases if they had an abnormal ECG

International Criteria for Athlete ECG Interpretation. All abnormal ECGs and all ECGs with contradictory interpretation between the original screening physician and the research team underwent additional review by 2 expert sports cardiologists, and in the event of a disagreement, the majority view was used. Athletes were considered to have an abnormal ECG if they had at least 1 ECG requiring further evaluation (abnormal or with ≥2 borderline findings) according to the International Criteria. If athletes had >1 abnormal ECG, only the first was included in the analyses. Athletes were considered isolated TWI V2–3 cases if they had an abnormal ECG with TWI ≥1 mm in depth in leads V 2 and V 3 and no other abnormal ECG findings according to the International Criteria and were aged ≥16 years (ie, the finding could not be considered a juvenile T‐wave pattern). In accordance with the International Criteria, athletes with a biphasic T wave in V 3 only were considered normal. ECGs of isolated TWI V2–3 cases underwent additional independent review by 2 members of the research team blinded as to sex and sport, with any discrepancies resolved by a third senior clinician reviewer. The presence of the following features was noted, many of which are associated with cardiomyopathies : Net negative QRS vector in lead V 3 (late R‐S transition); Bifid T waves, if the negative portion was deeper than −0.1 mV in leads V 2 and V 3 ; Deep TWI, defined as ≥−0.2 mV ; ST segment preceding the TWI V2–3 categorized as isoelectric, ascending convex, ascending concave, or depressed; J‐point elevation ≥0.1 mV; Low QRS voltages (<0.5 mV peak to peak) in all limb leads ; Pathological Q waves (Q/R ratio ≥0.25 or ≥40 ms in duration in ≥2 leads, excluding III and aVR) ; Prolonged S‐wave upstroke (terminal activation duration of QRS ≥55 ms from the nadir of the S wave to the end of the QRS) ; ≥1 ventricular ectopic beats; Epsilon waves (low‐amplitude signal between the end of the QRS complex and onset of the T wave in leads V 1 –V 3 ) ; Left‐axis deviation (−30 o to –90 o ) ; Complete RBBB) (rSR′ pattern in lead V 1 and an S wave wider than R wave in lead V 6 with QRS duration ≥120 ms) ; and Incomplete RBBB (rSR′ pattern in lead V1 and a qRS pattern in lead V 6 with QRS duration <120 ms). Sport disciplines included most Olympic and Paralympic sports (summer and winter), Australian football, cricket, football (soccer), and netball. Each athlete's sporting discipline was categorized as either skill, power, mixed, or endurance in accordance with the European Association of Preventive Cardiology position statement. Endurance sports included middle‐ and long‐distance running, cycling, rowing, canoeing, swimming, triathlon, and cross‐country skiing. Paralympic athletes were listed separately. Sex was determined on the basis of the medical records held by each sporting organization. Statistical Analysis Continuous variables were reported as means±SD and categorical variables were reported as percentages. Comparisons between proportions were made with a χ 2 test using 2×2 contingency tables and a 2‐sided test, with P <0.05 considered significant. A logistic regression analysis calculated odds ratios with 95% CIs for the odds of isolated TWI V2–3 adjusting for sex and sporting discipline (endurance versus nonendurance). All analyses were conducted using Prism version 10.4.0 (GraphPad Software, La Jolla, CA). Results The combined data set comprised 4423 athletes (40% female athletes, mean age at first screening, 19.7±4.5 years; Table ). Athletes in the cohort were predominantly White individuals, consistent with previously reported demographics of elite athletes in Australia. Isolated TWI V2–3 was found in 36 athletes aged ≥16 years: (27 [1.5%] female athletes, 9 [0.3%] male athletes; mean age at first screening, 21.3±4.5 years; Table ). There was 86% agreement between reviewers on cases for inclusion, with disagreement resolved by a third senior clinician. The finding was most common in female and endurance athletes (Table ). Follow‐up investigations were available for 34 of 36 athletes with TWI V2–3 , including: echocardiogram (n=30), cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (n=3), stress ECG (n=2), or subsequent normal ECG (n=13) (Table ). One (male) athlete refused further evaluation, and 1 (male) athlete had not yet completed follow‐up. After 6.4±2.6 years of follow‐up, no athletes with isolated TWI V2–3 were diagnosed with cardiac disease nor had a major cardiac event. Sex Differences Isolated TWI V2–3 was more common in female compared with male athletes, adjusting for sporting discipline (adjusted odds ratio, 4.2 [95% CI, 2.0–9.5]; Table ). Isolated TWI V2–3 was the most common abnormal ECG finding in female athletes' screening ECGs (36% of abnormal ECGs in female athletes compared with 13% in male athletes). The second and third most common abnormalities in female athletes were other abnormal TWI and ≥2 premature ventricular contractions. None of the female athletes with isolated TWI V2–3 had other ECG abnormalities on subsequent cardiac screening, and 70% had an earlier or later normal ECG. Two male athletes had later ECGs with other abnormalities (TWI in other leads, pathological Q waves). Overall, female athletes had a higher proportion of abnormal ECGs compared with male athletes (4.2% versus 2.6%, P =0.004; Table , with details of other ECG abnormalities stratified by sex in Table ). If TWI V2–3 was considered a normal finding in female athletes, female and male athletes would have similar proportions of abnormal ECGs (2.6% versus 2.6%, P =0.95). Sporting Discipline Differences All cases of isolated TWI V2–3 were in endurance (Figure [ ]) or mixed sport (Figure [ ]) athletes. Isolated TWI V2–3 was more common in endurance compared with nonendurance athletes, after adjusting for sex (adjusted odds ratio, 4.8 [95% CI, 2.5–9.5]; Table ). Other <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ECG</styled-content> Features Of athletes with TWI V2–3 , 69% had a net QRS vector that was negative in lead V 3 (Figure [ ], Table ). Bifid T waves were noted in 61%, deep TWI in 19%, and incomplete RBBB in 31%. The ST segment preceding TWI was either isoelectric (56%) or ascending convex (44%), although more commonly isoelectric in female athletes (67% versus 22%, P =0.02). J‐point elevation was present in 36% of athletes with TWI V2–3 but less common in female athletes compared with males (26% versus 67%, P =0.03). Voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy and right ventricular hypertrophy was uncommon in female athletes with TWI V2–3 but was present in the majority of male athletes (left ventricular hypertrophy: 4% versus 78%, P <0.0001; right ventricular hypertrophy: 7% versus 78%, P <0.0001; Table ). Discussion In a data set of 4423 athletes, we found that both being female and being an endurance athlete were independently associated with increased odds of isolated TWI V2–3 . This finding was not accompanied by any diagnoses of pathologic conditions at risk of SCD. Isolated TWI V2–3 was the most common abnormal finding in female athletes' screening ECGs and almost entirely accounted for the higher proportion of female athletes with an abnormal ECG compared with male athletes. Female Athletes Our results showing female athletes have a higher proportion of abnormal screening ECGs are consistent with previous studies using the International Criteria. , , Generally, the findings in these studies have not been matched by a higher number of diagnoses associated with SCD. The time and cost of follow‐up testing is one of the key burdens of screening, and thus reducing false positives is an important way to ensure that the benefits of screening outweigh the detriments. Importantly, the positive predictive value of ECG screening in detecting rare conditions associated with SCD is “exquisitely dependent” on the specificity of the interpretation criteria. The sensitivity and specificity of the International Criteria have been reported in White and Black athletes and are a major improvement on previous criteria in terms of diagnostic accuracy. However, the largest study is based on a predominantly male (95%) cohort of UK football players. To our knowledge, the overall sensitivity and specificity of the current athlete ECG interpretation criteria in a large cohort of female athletes has not been studied, and this would

TWI V2–3 is associated with arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and other cardiomyopathies. A study comparing 162 patients with ARVC against 129 healthy young controls with anterior TWI found that 81% of patients with ARVC had an abnormal ECG and anterior TWI was the most common ECG abnormality (51%). However, anterior TWI was less commonly an isolated finding in those with cardiomyopathy: of the patients with ARVC with anterior TWI, 77% had at least 1 other abnormal ECG feature. Consistent with our report, other recent studies presenting cardiac screening results do not include any examples of female athletes with isolated TWI V2–3 being diagnosed with ARVC. , , , , Our study found that female sex was strongly and independently associated with increased odds of isolated TWI V2–3 , adjusting for sporting discipline. Some smaller studies report a higher proportion (5%–8%) , , , of female athletes with TWI V2–3 , compared with 1.5% in our study. This difference may be the result of chance/natural variation in smaller sample sizes (n<1000). Malhotra et al found a higher proportion of TWI V2–3 in female compared with male athletes (2.1% versus 0.3%, P <0.0001), none of whom were diagnosed with ARVC after extensive investigation. Conversely, a large UK cohort of 11 168 male football (soccer) players screened at the age of 16 years reported diagnoses of ARVC in 2 male athletes: one had isolated TWI V2–3 on ECG (together with symptoms of palpitations/dizziness), and the other had a normal ECG and history and physical examination but an abnormal echocardiogram. In addition, an audit of cardiac screening in UK cricket reported 1 diagnosis of ARVC in a male player, who had isolated TWI V2–3 and a normal history and physical examination. As in previous studies, we found that the ST segment preceding TWI was more commonly isoelectric (than not) in female compared with male athletes with isolated TWI V2–3 (67% versus 22%, P =0.02). , We also found that J‐point elevation was less common in female athletes with TWI V2–3 compared with male athletes (26% versus 67%, P =0.03). Thus, our results are consistent with the findings of Malhotra et al, who suggest that a J point and ST segment in line with the onset of the QRS complex may be potential markers of disease in male athletes with anterior TWI but not in female athletes. Finocchiaro et al aimed to differentiate between benign TWI and ARVC and concluded that a J point <0.1 mV preceding anterior TWI was not a useful way to differentiate physiology from pathology. They found that a J point <0.1 mV was common in those with ARVC and in the group of healthy young people (including athletes) with anterior TWI. However, consideration of the J point and ST segment is included in the 2024 European Task Force criteria, which classifies TWI in the right precordial leads in the absence of complete RBBB and not preceded by J‐point/ST‐segment elevation , as a major criterion for ARVC diagnosis. Interestingly, we found that isolated TWI V2–3 in some female athletes was inconsistent (Table ). This could be due to differences in conditioning if this is a physiological adaptation or differences in lead placement. Lead placement and breast tissue have been suggested as possible explanations for sex differences in isolated TWI V2–3 . , , , The prevalence of anterior TWI in prepubertal children has been shown to be similar in boys and girls, which supports the theory that breast tissue in older female athletes could affect lead placement. Many athletes in our study were screened in sporting settings (eg, the training ground), sometimes without optimal privacy. In these situations, female athletes may have left their sports bra on during ECG recording, potentially complicating accurate lead placement. Lead placement can also cause a net negative QRS vector, which we found was numerically lower in female cases with TWI V2–3 , although this difference did not reach statistical significance. Alternatively, it is possible that anterior T‐wave changes could reflect right ventricular remodeling that is specific to the female sex. That is, this ECG finding could reflect the actual adaptive right ventricular physiology that occurs in female athletes, especially female endurance athletes. Female athletes are underrepresented in research describing exercise‐induced cardiac remodeling and a more detailed study using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging would be required to answer this question. Exercise‐induced cardiac remodeling in female athletes may also cause rotation changes of the heart within a smaller thoracic cavity in female athletes, leading to changes on the ECG. Endurance Athletes We found isolated TWI V2–3 was nearly 5 times as common in endurance athletes, after adjusting for sex. This is consistent with previous studies, which have reported this ECG finding as being at least 3 times more common in endurance compared with nonendurance athletes. , , A study by Brosnan et al of 1261 athletes screened with ECG found TWI up to V 3 was present in 6% of endurance athletes compared with 0.1% of nonendurance athletes. Looking for a suggested explanation, in a later study, Brosnan et al used cardiac magnetic resonance imaging to show that TWI V2–3 in healthy endurance athletes (93% male athletes) was associated with lateral displacement of the right ventricle toward the left axilla. This study compared 68 endurance athletes with 41 controls and measured cardiac displacement and orientation within the thorax using horizontal long‐axis images. Smaller thoracic size was found to contribute, which could be a factor in female athletes. Our data provide supportive electrocardiographic evidence of this phenomenon. Specifically, more than two thirds of athletes in this cohort with TWI V2–3 demonstrated a negative net QRS vector in V 3 . This finding among healthy athletes is likely explained by anatomic counterclockwise rotation of the heart due to right ventricular–predominant exercise‐induced dilation. While future work examining the relationship between net QRS vector and TWI inversion patterns is warranted, this pattern may serve as an additional ECG finding to supporting the benign nature of TWI V2–3 among endurance athletes. Recommendations for Changes to Athlete <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">ECG</styled-content> Criteria Our findings support that isolated TWI V2–3 may be considered a normal ECG finding in asymptomatic female athletes, which mirrors the 2025 expert opinion statement of the Italian Society of Sports Cardiology and suggestions in previous studies. , , This has been identified as an area for consideration in updates to athlete ECG interpretation criteria. It is likely that recognizing isolated TWI V2–3 as a normal finding would lower the false‐positive rate of ECG screening in female athletes without any significant loss in sensitivity for conditions at risk of SCD. Strengths and Limitations A key strength of this data set is that it includes a large number and proportion of elite female athletes. Female athletes are underrepresented in sports cardiology research, including data from preparticipation screening programs. , In addition, this data set is composed of elite athletes at a high competitive level. The vast majority were tier 3 (highly trained/national level), tier 4 (elite/international level), or tier 5 (world class). Athletes at these higher levels generally train more and at higher intensity, which may be relevant to the degree of cardiac remodeling evident on their screening ECGs (especially for endurance athletes). This was a real‐world study with a number of limitations. First, data were limited to the records available at participating sporting organizations, and most were collected retrospectively. It is possible that these records were incomplete and that some athlete screening ECGs and follow‐up tests were performed but not included. However, we used our best endeavors to work with sports medicine staff at participating organizations to identify all relevant records, particularly for athletes requiring further evaluation. Second, follow‐up details were not available for 2 (male) isolated TWI V2–3 cases. It is therefore possible that either or both of these cases had a clinically relevant diagnosis that was not identified. Finally, the evaluation for cardiomyopathy was determined by treating physicians and primarily limited to echocardiogram alone. Therefore, it is possible that if all athletes with isolated TWI V2–3 were investigated more comprehensively (eg, with Holter, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, signal‐averaged ECG and stress ECG) or followed for a longer period, some could be diagnosed with pathology. Conclusions Isolated TWI V2–3 was 4 times more common in female athletes compared with male athletes and 5 times more common in endurance athletes. This finding was not associated with pathologic conditions at risk of sudden death. Isolated TWI V2–3 was the most common ECG abnormality in female athletes and accounted for the higher proportion of abnormal ECGs in female athletes. Results from this large data set are consistent with previous studies and support that isolated TWI V2–3 may be considered a normal ECG finding in asymptomatic female athletes. These results may inform future ECG interpretation criteria in athletes.
